sources.entry: mssql-python - Official Microsoft driver for SQL Server and Azure SQL, built on ODBC for high performance.

summary.one_liner: mssql-python is Microsoft's official Python DB API 2.0 driver for SQL Server, Azure SQL Database and Azure SQL Managed Instance, connecting directly via DDBC without an external driver manager.
summary.what_it_does: Provides a Python module (imported as mssql_python) for connecting to Microsoft SQL Server and Azure SQL family databases, with connection management, query execution and transaction handling (commit/rollback). It follows the DB API 2.0 specification with connection and cursor objects, parameter placeholders, and a consistent set of exceptions. It supports Microsoft Entra ID authentication methods (username/password, managed identity, interactive browser, device code, integrated, default) across Windows, macOS and Linux. Built-in connection pooling is enabled by default and reuses connections with validation on checkout. Text parameters are always sent as UTF-16LE (SQL_C_WCHAR), and setdecoding() controls how results are read. Bulk copy and an alternate Rust ODBC provider come from a companion package, mssql-python-rs.
use_cases: connect Python applications to SQL Server
query Azure SQL Database from Python
connect to Azure SQL Managed Instance with Entra ID login
run parameterized SQL queries with transactions
pooled database connections for web services
managed identity authentication to Azure SQL
notable: Direct Database Connectivity without requiring an external ODBC driver manager
Pooled checkout validates reused connections with a bounded timeout
Opt-in alternate native ODBC provider selection via environment variable or module property
Conda candidate package bundles the ODBC payload (not publicly released per README)
Performance profiler for contributors, compiled out of released wheels
caveats: Requires Python 3.10 or newer; SUSE ARM64 is not supported.
Linux installs need system libraries such as libltdl and krb5; macOS encrypted connections need Homebrew OpenSSL.
Interactive and device-code auth share one signed-in identity per process, so it is not suitable for isolating multiple end users; bring-your-own tokens must be refreshed by the application.
